summary: Mandarin Chinese is the standard language of China and Taiwan and has more native speakers than any other language. Words never change their form; tones distinguish meanings; it is written in characters, and pinyin is the Latin spelling used for learning.

typology.why: No endings at all: 我吃, 他吃, 我们吃 — 吃 never changes. Time, number and questions are shown by separate words (了, 三个, 吗) and by word order.
typology.alsoShows: New words are mostly compounds of old ones: 电 ‘electric’ + 脑 ‘brain’ = 电脑 ‘computer’.

facts.label: Script
facts.value: Chinese characters — simplified (mainland China, Singapore) or traditional (Taiwan, Hong Kong); pinyin for pronunciation

facts.label: Where
facts.value: China, Taiwan, Singapore and Chinese communities worldwide

peculiarities.title: Tones
peculiarities.text: Every syllable has a tone: mā (high), má (rising), mǎ (low), mà (falling), ma (neutral). 妈 mā ‘mother’ and 马 mǎ ‘horse’ differ only in tone.

peculiarities.title: Measure words
peculiarities.text: Between a number (or 这/那) and a noun comes a measure word: 一个人, 三本书.

peculiarities.title: No tenses
peculiarities.text: Verbs do not change; time words (昨天) and particles (了, 过) say when and whether something happened.

peculiarities.title: Characters
peculiarities.text: Each character is a syllable with a meaning; you learn them through the words that contain them.

quiz.why: Words never change; grammar is word order and small separate words.

quiz.q: What tells 妈 mā ‘mother’ from 马 mǎ ‘horse’?
What comes between a number and a noun?

notes.text: Almost everything Greek inflects disappears: no genders, no cases, no verb endings, no articles. The new things are tones (the Greek accent is stress, not a pitch that changes the word) and measure words. A gift from Greek: Chinese b, d, g are unaspirated like Greek π, τ, κ, while p, t, k carry a strong puff of air, and Chinese h is close to Greek χ in χαρά. Chinese has no θ or δ, characters have no capital letters and no final forms like ς, and the speaker’s sex never shows (κουρασμένος / κουρασμένη — both 我累了).

The order subject – verb – object matches English (我是学生 ‘I am a student’), and English is already fairly analytic, so grammar without endings feels natural. Watch out for pinyin letters with values unlike English (q, x, zh, c, ü), for the missing ‘th’ sounds, and for English intonation: in Chinese the pitch belongs to each word, so a question is made with 吗, not by raising the voice. Characters have no capital letters; names are capitalised only in pinyin.

Your German compounds help a lot: Chinese builds words the same way (手机 ‘hand machine’ — the German Handy; 电话 ‘electric speech’). German ü is pinyin ü (女 nǚ), the ach-Laut is close to Chinese h, the ich-Laut close to x. Measure words have small German cousins — ein Blatt Papier, eine Tasse Kaffee, zwei Stück Kuchen — but in Chinese every counted noun needs one. Forget V2: the Chinese verb never moves to second place (明天我去 or 我明天去, never *明天去我). Syllables end only in a vowel, -n, -ng or -r, so there is nothing to devoice, and nouns are not capitalised — characters have no case.

Like Russian, Chinese has no articles. Russian drops ‘to be’ in the present (Я студент); Chinese needs 是 between two nouns (我是学生) but, like Russian, uses none before adjectives (她很高 ~ Она высокая). Russian ш is close to Chinese sh, щ to x, and your feel for verbal aspect (perfective / imperfective) will help with 了 and 过. New: no hard / soft consonant pairs, no cases, no word stress, no capital letters, syllables that end only in a vowel, -n, -ng or -r (nothing to devoice), and the speaker’s sex never shows (я устал / устала — both 我累了).

Turkish is the opposite technique — long words built from suffixes — yet many habits carry over: no gender (o = he / she / it, just like spoken tā), no ‘the’ (bir works like 一 + measure word), no plural after a number (iki kitap ~ 两本书), modifiers before the noun, and a question particle (mı ~ 吗). Unlike Turkish suffixes, Chinese particles never follow vowel harmony: 吗 is always 吗. What remains different is the order — Chinese puts the verb before the object (SVO) — and Chinese has no evidential like -miş: ‘I hear that …’ is said with words. Characters have no capital letters, there are no double consonants, and syllables end only in a vowel, -n, -ng or -r.

Spanish ser / estar prepare you for 是 / 在, and the SVO order matches. Everything else that changes in Spanish — gender, plural, verb endings, the subjunctive — is absent: a Chinese verb stays the same after ‘I want …’ or ‘so that …’. New are tones and measure words; characters have no capital letters, and Chinese has no θ.

French is SVO like Chinese and has no strong word stress, which suits the even beat of Chinese syllables; but gender, articles, conjugation and the subjunctive all disappear. French nasal vowels have no Chinese counterpart: in an / ang the n and ng are real consonants. Pinyin ü is French u (女 nǚ), and Chinese r is not the French r from the back of the throat. Characters have no capital letters.

Hindi’s aspirated / unaspirated pairs (प / फ, क / ख) are exactly Chinese b / p and g / k, and its retroflex consonants give a feel for the curled tongue of zh, ch, sh. But Chinese has no gender, no verb endings and no subject–object–verb order: the object follows the verb (我吃饭). Nasal vowels and double consonants do not exist, and the speaker’s sex never shows in the verb (मैं थका / थकी हूँ — both 我累了).

Persian has no gender either, and u is ‘he’ and ‘she’, as tā is in speech; Persian tā even works as an optional classifier (do tā ketāb ~ 两本书). New: tones; characters that never join or change shape; the object after the verb; and modifiers before the noun — the reverse of the ezafe (ketāb-e man ~ 我的书). Chinese has no uvular q and no double consonants: pinyin q is an aspirated, ‘ch’-like sound.

Marathi’s aspirated / unaspirated pairs match Chinese b / p, d / t, g / k, and its आपण / आम्ही split is Chinese 咱们 / 我们. Like Marathi, Chinese puts modifiers before the noun and has a question particle (का ~ 吗). New: tones, no gender, no endings, the object after the verb, no double consonants — and the speaker’s sex never shows in the verb.

Arabic builds words from roots and patterns; Chinese builds them by compounding whole syllables (电 + 话 = 电话) and never changes a word inside. Characters do not join or change shape by position, and there is no dual, no gender and no case; Chinese needs 是 between two nouns where Arabic needs nothing. Pharyngeal and emphatic consonants, double consonants and long vowels play no role — tones do. Pinyin q is not Arabic q but an aspirated, ‘ch’-like sound, and there are no θ / ð sounds.

Hebrew roots (k-t-v) have no Chinese counterpart: words are compounds of syllables (电 + 话 = 电话) and never change inside. Like Hebrew, Chinese puts no verb before adjectives (房子很大 ~ ha-bayit gadol), but it needs 是 between two nouns. Characters have no final forms (unlike ך ם ן ף ץ), and gender disappears even from ‘you’ (ata / at — 你).

Japanese gives you a head start: kanji are Chinese characters (学生, 电话 ~ 電話), counters work like measure words, the topic comes first, and the question particle か matches 吗. New: tones instead of pitch accent, simplified character forms (话 for 話), and SVO order — the object follows the verb (我吃饭). Some kanji mislead: Japanese 手紙 is ‘letter’, Chinese 手纸 is toilet paper. Long vowels and double consonants (おばあさん, きって) play no role in Chinese.

Many Korean words are Sino-Korean and close to their Chinese source (학생 haksaeng ~ 学生 xuésheng, 전화 jeonhwa ~ 电话 diànhuà), and counters, topic-first order and verb-like adjectives are familiar. New: tones, characters instead of Hangul, SVO order (the object after the verb), and no speech levels — politeness is 您, 请 and titles, not verb endings.

Finnish has no gender (hän ~ spoken tā) and no articles, but its fifteen cases, vowel harmony, consonant gradation and long vowels and consonants all disappear: a Chinese word never changes, and length means nothing. What is new is pitch — tones tell words apart. Characters have no capital letters.

Hungarian puts the family name first (Kovács János ~ 王小明), writes dates big to small (2026. május 1. ~ 2026年五月一号), has no gender (ő ~ tā), keeps the noun singular after numbers (két könyv ~ 两本书) and even has two words for ‘two’ (két / kettő ~ 两 / 二). Cases, vowel harmony, long vowels and double consonants disappear, and characters have no capital letters; tones are new.

Swahili is SVO, so the basic order is familiar, but Chinese tones are new. Noun classes and their agreement disappear — Chinese has measure words instead, which also sort nouns by kind. Chinese counts the hours from midnight, not from 6 a.m.; it has no ‘th’ sounds (as in thelathini), and characters have no capital letters.

Luganda is a tone language too, so pitch that tells words apart is familiar; Chinese tones are contours on every syllable. Noun classes, agreement and verb prefixes disappear — Chinese words never change, and measure words sort nouns by kind. The SVO order matches, but Chinese puts adjectives, numbers and possessors before the noun, Luganda after it. Characters have no capital letters.

Vietnamese is the closest type of all: isolating, tonal, SVO, with classifiers, verb-like adjectives and many Sino-Vietnamese words (học sinh ~ 学生, điện thoại ~ 电话). Two differences matter: Chinese puts modifiers before the noun (我的书, 大房子), Vietnamese after it (sách của tôi, nhà to); and Chinese is written in characters, with pinyin only as a learner’s aid; characters have no capital letters.

Inuktitut is the opposite extreme: one long word can be a whole sentence, built from a stem and many suffixes. Chinese words are short and never change; every meaning is a separate word in a fixed order. Verb–object words such as 吃饭 ‘eat-meal’ look like incorporation but are two words that can be split (吃了饭). Pinyin q is not the Inuktitut uvular q but an aspirated, ‘ch’-like sound.
